author: Brianna Kelly
title: Congress delays federal hemp ban, continues to explore permanent solution - NewsBreak
text:
By Brianna Kelly ,
4 hours ago
A looming federal hemp ban that’s expected to derail Minnesota’s booming THC beverage industry has been delayed a month as members of Congress work to find long-term solution.
On Tuesday, the U.S. House of Representatives voted 370-48 in favor of a short-term government funding bill, which sailed through the Senate almost a month ago. It includes a provision to delay the federal ban on hemp-derived THC products until Dec. 11, compared to its original effective date of Nov. 12.
The measure to stave off a government shutdown right before the midterm elections now heads to President Donald Trump’s desk. He’s expected to sign it.
A sign inside a Total Wine store informing shoppers about the impending THC ban.Bring Me The News
Similarly, a provision to outlaw hemp products containing more than 0.4 milligrams of THC was included at the last minute in legislation that narrowly passed to end the longest-running government shutdown last November.
Championed by Republican Sen. Mitch McConnell of Kentucky, the proposal that’s now set to become law sought to close a so-called loophole in the 2018 Farm Bill that legalized hemp nationwide and enabled manufacturers to create intoxicating products with legal amounts of THC from hemp.
Democratic Sens. Amy Klobuchar and Tina Smith have worked with Republican Sen. Rand Paul of Kentucky in their efforts to stop the restrictions from taking effect .
The one-month delay allows the industry to keep moving forward while Congress works on a long-term solution, according to Minnesota’s pair of senators.
“Adults should have the freedom to purchase a THC beverage if they want to,” Smith said in a statement Tuesday. “Minnesota has created one of the strongest, most carefully regulated systems in the country to allow the sale of hemp products.
“The initial ban set to take place was ill-advised and would have hurt both hemp farmers and Minnesota breweries alike.”
Low-dose, hemp-derived THC seltzers have buoyed many Minnesota breweries grappling with skyrocketing costs and plummeting beer sales in recent years.
More than 5,300 retailers across Minnesota are licensed to sell clearly labeled hemp-derived THC products, many of which are distributed to other states as well.
Opponents claim that the beverages, gummies, chocolates, and other products containing hemp-derived are too attractive and accessible to children.

On Tuesday, the U.S. House of Representatives voted 370-48 in favor of a short-term government funding bill, which sailed through the Senate almost a month ago. It includes a provision to delay the federal ban on hemp-derived THC products until Dec. 11, compared to its original effective date of Nov. 12.
